title: International Filter Co. v. Conroe Gin, Ice & Light Co.
lead: Conroe Gin signed a water-filter order that required approval at the manufacturer’s Chicago office. The manufacturer’s executive approved it, but Conroe Gin later tried to cancel, making the written approval clause—and whether notice was also necessary—the center of the dispute.

actors.name: International Filter Company
actors.role: Illinois water-purification equipment manufacturer, plaintiff, and party seeking review.

actors.name: Conroe Gin, Ice & Light Company
actors.role: Texas ice manufacturer and proposed equipment buyer.

actors.name: Henry Thompson
actors.role: Conroe Gin’s manager who signed the order.

actors.name: P. N. Engel
actors.role: International Filter executive who endorsed the order in Chicago.

proceedings: The trial court entered judgment for Conroe Gin after a bench trial, and the Court of Civil Appeals affirmed. The Commission of Appeals recommended reversal and remand to the intermediate court for unresolved questions; the Texas Supreme Court adopted that disposition.
limits: The formation rulings did not resolve every issue in the breach action or produce a final damages award. The reported transaction occurred in 1920 and was analyzed under common-law formation principles; the decision does not apply modern Uniform Commercial Code rules.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A traveling salesman presents a conditional equipment proposal
sections.cue: What did the paper require before it became a contract?
paragraphs: International Filter Company manufactured water-purification equipment in Illinois, with its principal office in Chicago. Conroe Gin, Ice & Light Company manufactured ice in Conroe, Texas. On February 10, 1920, International Filter’s traveling representative, W. W. Waterman, presented a written proposal to Conroe Gin’s manager, Henry Thompson.

The paper described a No. 2 Junior steel-tank water softener and filter for $1,230, to be furnished free on board (f.o.b.) Chicago. Suitability for Conroe Gin’s water would be determined from a sample. The proposal said it would become a contract when accepted by the purchaser and approved by an International Filter executive officer at the Chicago office. Changes required an approved supplementary agreement signed by both parties. The proposal also called for prompt acceptance and permitted change without notice if acceptance was not prompt.

Thompson signed for Conroe Gin that day using an acceptance notation. The paper requested shipment by March 10 and went to Chicago. Thompson later testified that he had told Waterman when signing that prompt notification was required. Whether that claimed oral direction added a condition would become disputed.

sections.title: An executive approves, and the company begins arranging performance
sections.cue: What occurred before Conroe Gin tried to cancel?
paragraphs: On February 13, P. N. Engel, described in the opinion as International Filter’s president and vice president, placed a dated approval on the paper in Chicago. On February 14, the company mailed Conroe Gin a letter acknowledging and thanking it for the order, identifying the equipment and electrical specifications, and referring to shipment on March 10. It requested a prompt water sample so the company could analyze the water before shipping. Conroe Gin received the letter in due course.

Conroe Gin attempted to cancel by letter on February 28. International Filter replied on March 2, denied that the buyer had a right to cancel, and insisted on performance. Conroe Gin reiterated its cancellation position on March 4. International Filter then sued for breach.

sections.title: Conroe Gin wins the first two rounds on formation and other issues
sections.cue: What arguments reached the reviewing court?
paragraphs: Conroe Gin argued that neither Engel’s endorsement nor the February 14 letter was the executive approval contemplated by the proposal. It also argued that notice of approval was essential and had not been given, relying both on its reading of the form and Thompson’s testimony about his oral demand for prompt notification.

After a trial without a jury, the trial court entered judgment for Conroe Gin, finding for it on formation and other material issues. The Court of Civil Appeals affirmed. That court did recognize Engel’s endorsement as approval within the writing’s terms; the asserted need for notice remained the central formation obstacle. International Filter sought further review.

sections.title: The signed order gives the manufacturer the power to accept
sections.cue: Why was Conroe Gin the offeror despite the form’s labels?
paragraphs: The Commission of Appeals treated the signed document sent to Chicago as Conroe Gin’s offer to purchase. International Filter had drafted the form and called it a proposal, and Conroe Gin had signed language of acceptance. But the form reserved an additional executive act. Conroe Gin’s signature therefore supplied the operative offer, and International Filter could accept through the specified approval.

Engel’s dated endorsement was an approval by an executive officer at the designated office. No additional ritual was necessary. The question was whether separate communication of that approval was also required.

The court drew on Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co., a formation decision illustrating an offeror’s power to make a specified act sufficient acceptance. Although notice ordinarily protects an offeror seeking a return promise, an offeror can dispense with notice by selecting another sufficient method. Conroe Gin’s signed writing said the contract arose upon executive approval in Chicago. Requiring notice to arrive in Conroe would add a condition and change the specified time and place of formation.

The prompt-acceptance clause governed the timing of approval, not an additional form of acceptance or notification. The writing was unambiguous, so the court applied its terms despite Thompson’s claimed oral instruction. That reasoning concerned waiver of notice in this transaction; it did not eliminate the ordinary notice rule for offers that retain it.

sections.title: The acknowledgment would communicate approval even if notice were required
sections.cue: Why did the February 14 letter provide an alternative ground?
paragraphs: The court also concluded that the acknowledgment sufficiently notified Conroe Gin of approval if notification was necessary. Engel’s endorsement had already performed the approval act; the letter’s function was to communicate that act. A notice could do so by reasonable implication without using a prescribed formula.

The letter thanked Conroe Gin for the specific order, described the planned shipment, and requested a sample necessary to perform. A reasonable recipient would understand that International Filter had approved the order. The court further observed that reliance on such a letter might prevent the company from later denying approval. That observation was hypothetical; the reported facts did not establish actual reliance by Conroe Gin.

Nor did waiving notice make an entirely unexpressed intention enough. Engel had made the observable written endorsement that the offer selected. The distinction matters when comparing White, where a builder’s general preparations did not express acceptance of the proposed job: the offer and circumstances must make the offeree’s actual conduct sufficient assent.

sections.title: The buyer’s formation defenses fail, but the action is not finished
sections.cue: What judgment did the Texas Supreme Court adopt?
paragraphs: The Commission of Appeals recommended reversing the Court of Civil Appeals and returning the case to that court for questions properly presented but not previously decided. On December 10, 1925, Chief Justice Cureton, acting for the Texas Supreme Court, adopted that disposition.

International Filter prevailed on the formation questions. It did not receive a final damages award from the reviewing court, and unresolved issues in the breach action remained for the intermediate appellate court.
